readerTitle: Why your best idea shouldn't wait until the last line
caseNote: 실제 사례 (McKinsey의 Barbara Minto) + 실제 관찰 (신문 기사의 역피라미드) + 가상 적용 (레스토랑, 소프트웨어 회사)
insight: 보고는 내가 일한 순서가 아니라 상대가 결정하는 데 필요한 순서로 쓴다. 결론을 먼저 주면 나머지 내용은 그 결론을 판단하는 근거가 된다.
misconception: 배경부터 차근차근 설명해야 상대가 결론을 납득한다. 결론을 먼저 말하면 성급하거나 무례해 보인다.

sources.text: Minto, B. The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking. (Minto가 McKinsey에서 개발한 글쓰기 방법)
신문 기사 작성의 역피라미드(inverted pyramid) 관행: 저널리즘 교과서의 표준 설명
레스토랑과 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Barbara Minto가 McKinsey에 합류한 시기(1960년대, 흔히 1963년으로 소개)와 컨설턴트 글쓰기 교육을 맡았다는 내용을 Minto 공식 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 "in the 1960s"로만 적었습니다.
『The Pyramid Principle』의 최초 출간 연도는 판본마다 다르게 소개됩니다. 카드에는 연도를 적지 않았습니다.
Minto가 본 보고서들이 '분석한 순서대로' 쓰였다는 진단은 그녀의 책과 인터뷰에서 소개되는 일반적 설명입니다. 구체적 수치나 인용은 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전에 표현을 확인하세요.
레스토랑 사례 수치는 가상입니다: 공급업체 가격 15% 인상, 대체 업체로 월 약 $600 절약. 계산 의존성 없음.

cards.title: Why your best idea shouldn't wait until the last line
body: A consultant spends weeks on a project. The report walks through every step: the data collected, the analyses run, the dead ends explored. The recommendation shows up at the very end.
In the 1960s, Barbara Minto, a writing coach at McKinsey, kept seeing reports built this way. Clients paying for an answer had to dig to find it.

image.label: A thick report with the answer hidden on the last page
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두꺼운 보고서 더미를 넘기는 바쁜 임원의 손. 맨 마지막 페이지에서만 작은 전구(답)가 빛남. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your fish supplier just raised prices.
body: You manage a busy restaurant. Your fish supplier raised prices 15%. You tested a new supplier, the chef likes the quality, and switching saves about $600 a month. You need the owner's approval.
The owner reads messages on a phone between services. How do you open your message?

options.text: "Last month our supplier told us prices were going up, so I started looking around..."
options.feedback: It feels thorough and respectful. But the owner must read the whole story before learning what you want, and may stop halfway.

options.text: "I recommend we switch fish suppliers next month. It saves about $600 a month, and the chef approved the quality."
options.feedback: The owner knows the ask and the main reasons in two lines. Everything after that is evidence they can check or skip.

options.text: "Quick question about suppliers. Do you have ten minutes to talk today?"
options.feedback: A call can help on big decisions. But this tells the owner nothing yet and adds a meeting to a full day.

cards.title: Writers report in the order they worked.
body: Minto's diagnosis was simple. People write things down in the order they discovered them: background, then analysis, then conclusion. That order makes sense to the writer, who lived through it.

The reader didn't. They have to hold every detail in their head without knowing what it's for. Her fix was to flip the order: state the main point first, then give the reasons that support it. She later built this into a method taught widely to consultants, and a book, *The Pyramid Principle*.

cards.title: Lead with the answer
body: **Lead with the answer** means your first sentence says what you conclude or what you want the reader to decide. The background and evidence come after.
It's a shift from the writer's order to the reader's order. The writer asks, "What did I do?" The reader asks, "What do you need from me, and why should I agree?"

image.label: Two arrows: writer's order versus reader's order
image.brief: 두 줄 비교 인포그래픽. 위쪽 "Writer's order": Background → Analysis → Answer (답이 맨 끝, 작게). 아래쪽 "Reader's order": Answer → Reasons → Details (답이 맨 앞, 크게 강조). 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: The answer turns details into evidence.
body: When readers know the conclusion first, every fact that follows has a job. They can judge it: does this support the answer or not?
It also respects how attention works. People read the opening most closely. A busy reader who stops early still leaves with the point.
cards.callout: Newspapers have long done the same. The *inverted pyramid* puts the most important facts in the first paragraph, so a reader who quits early still knows the story.

cards.title: Not just for reports.
list: **Email subject lines:** "Approve new fish supplier by Friday" beats "Supplier update"
**Meetings:** open with the decision you need, not a recap
**Hallway updates:** "We're on track, one risk" before the details
**Bad news:** say what happened first, then why
cards.callout: In every case, the first line answers: what do you need from me?

cards.title: Leading with the answer has conditions.
body: You need an answer first. If you don't have one yet, say so up front: "No recommendation yet. I need one more number by Thursday." That is still leading with the point.

A surprising or unwelcome answer can make a skeptical reader stop listening. Keep it first, but name the shared goal in the same breath: "To protect margins, I recommend we raise prices." And leading doesn't mean skipping the evidence. It means putting it second.

cards.title: Now it's a software launch.
body: You lead product at a software company. Testing found a bug that could corrupt data for your largest customer on launch day. The fix takes four days. You think launch should move one week.
Your CEO reads chat messages between meetings. Which message do you send?

options.text: "Heads up: testing turned up something in the data sync. Details below..." followed by the full test log
options.feedback: The evidence is all there, but the CEO must dig through logs to learn there is a decision to make, and might miss it.

options.text: "Recommend moving launch one week. A bug could corrupt our largest customer's data; the fix takes four days. Need your OK by 3 pm."
options.feedback: Decision, reason and deadline in one message. The CEO can approve in seconds or ask for the logs.

options.text: "We might need to talk about the launch date at some point."
options.feedback: It flags a problem without alarm. But it hides the recommendation and the urgency, so the decision may slip past the deadline.

cards.title: Put the answer where the reader looks first.
body: Start with your conclusion or your ask. Then give the reasons. Then the details, for anyone who wants them.
**Try it today:** open the last important email you sent. Move its key sentence to the top and see how much of the rest you still need.
